screens.title: Behavioral Patterns — Observer and Strategy
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll explore two essential behavioral patterns that control how objects communicate and change behavior. First, Observer establishes a one-to-many relationship so a subject can notify many observers when its state changes. This is the backbone of event-driven systems and GUIs where decoupled updates are required. Second, Strategy isolates algorithms behind a common interface so a client can swap behaviors at runtime without modifying its own code. We'll look closely at Java examples for each pattern and practical use cases where they improve flexibility. You'll see a NewsAgency and news channels demonstrating Observer, and a ShoppingCart with discount strategies demonstrating Strategy. We'll also discuss common mistakes: uncontrolled observer lists leading to memory leaks and overuse of Strategy when algorithms are stable. By the end you'll be able to choose between notifying dependents and encapsulating algorithms, and implement both patterns in small, testable Java classes. Consider how your current projects handle notifications and algorithm choices — could a pattern reduce conditional logic or tighten coupling? That question will guide the hands-on tasks we present next.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus on practical implementation and design judgement. First, you'll implement the Observer pattern so a subject can notify multiple observers when its state changes. That matters in event-driven code and GUIs where many components react to a single source without tight coupling. Second, you'll identify appropriate use cases for Observer, such as subscriptions, live feeds, or GUI listeners, and understand the memory-care required when registering and removing observers. Each objective emphasizes both the how and the why. Third, you'll implement the Strategy pattern to encapsulate algorithms and make them interchangeable, reducing conditional branches and improving testability. Fourth, you'll learn to decide between Observer and Strategy by contrasting their roles: Observer manages communication among objects, Strategy manages internal algorithm choice. The skills include writing Java interfaces, concrete implementations, and small client classes that compose patterns safely. You'll practice with live code examples and guided tasks to ensure you can both apply the patterns and recognize when they are unnecessary overhead.

screens.title: Behavioral Patterns — What they are and why they matter
screens.narratorSegment: Behavioral patterns focus on object interaction and the assignment of responsibilities. They are not about creating objects or arranging structure; they are about how objects collaborate at runtime. The core claim is simple: by standardizing interaction through small, focused interfaces, your code becomes easier to change and reason about. For example, Observer standardizes notification so subjects and observers are decoupled; Strategy standardizes algorithm selection so clients delegate behavior. A concrete example: in a GUI, an event source does not need to know every listener type—listeners implement a common interface and register themselves. A common misconception is that patterns are a silver bullet that solve all coupling problems. In reality, misuse can add unnecessary indirection: use Strategy only when algorithms interchange or when clients must vary behavior. Similarly, Observer can introduce hidden memory retention if observers are not removed. To apply these patterns, learn their vocabulary: Subject and Observer for publish-subscribe, Strategy and Context for interchangeable algorithms. Practice by writing small interfaces first, then minimal concrete implementations that are easy to test. Which responsibilities in your code could be split into a small interface and a set of interchangeable behaviors?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Behavioral patterns describe how objects interact and delegate responsibilities to support flexible, testable code.

content.html:
Core Concept
Behavioral patterns organize communication
They describe how objects distribute responsibility and communicate at runtime through small, well-defined interfaces.
Definition: Behavioral patterns focus on algorithms and object interaction roles.
Why it matters: They reduce conditional code and keep classes single responsibility and testable.
Misconception: Avoid overusing patterns; indirection can add complexity when requirements are stable.
Key Takeaway

Introduce small interfaces to separate communication and algorithms. Use patterns when they reduce conditional logic or coupling.

Analogy: Orchestra
Think of objects as musicians. Behavioral patterns are the conductor's sheet music: they define how players coordinate without directly knowing each other's details.
Quick checklist
  • Is behavior likely to change or be swapped? Consider Strategy.
  • Do many components react to one source? Consider Observer.
  • Can interfaces make testing easier? Prefer small interfaces.
Reflect: pick one place in your code where responsibilities could be split into an interface and a set of strategies or observers.

screens.title: Observer pattern — Roles and mechanics
screens.narratorSegment: The Observer pattern defines a one-to-many dependency so that when one object changes state, all its dependents are notified automatically. The vocabulary matters: the Subject (or Publisher) holds a list of Observers (Subscribers). Observers implement a common update method that the Subject calls when its state changes. A concrete example from the chapter is a NewsAgency subject and NewsChannel observers. When NewsAgency. setNews() updates state it calls notifyObservers(), and each NewsChannel. update() handles the message. This promotes loose coupling because the Subject depends only on the Observer interface, not concrete types. A common mistake is leaving observers registered after they are no longer needed; that can keep objects alive and cause memory leaks in long-running applications. Another practical note: choose the notification payload carefully — sending minimal, stable data reduces the need to change both Subject and Observers. To implement Observer in Java, create Subject and Observer interfaces, a concrete subject that maintains a list of observers, and concrete observers that register themselves. Test by registering several observers, updating state, and confirming each observer received the update. What cleanup steps will you include to avoid leaks?

keyIdea.title: Observer roles
keyIdea.text: Subject maintains observers and notifies them; Observers respond through a shared update interface, enabling loose coupling.

content.html:
Definition
Observer pattern mechanics
Subject registers observers, and when the Subject's state changes it calls update on each Observer. This decouples the Subject from concrete observer classes.
Subject: holds observers and notifies them.
Observer: interface that defines update behavior.
Concrete implementations: Subjects store state; observers react to notifications.
Key Takeaway

Use Observer when many components must react to a single changing source without tight coupling or direct references.

Concrete example
NewsAgency acts as Subject. NewsChannel implements Observer.update(String message) and registers with the agency. When setNews runs, notifyObservers calls update on every channel.
Common mistake
Failing to remove observers keeps references alive and causes memory leaks in long-running programs.
Mnemonic: "One-to-many, update-to-all." Keep observer lists explicit and manage their lifecycle.

screens.title: Observer — NewsAgency example walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Let's step through the NewsAgency and NewsChannel example to see Observer in practice. The Subject interface declares registerObserver, removeObserver, and notifyObservers. NewsAgency keeps a List of Observer and a news state. When setNews is called it assigns the new string and calls notifyObservers, which iterates over the list and invokes update on each Observer. NewsChannel implements update to print or otherwise react to the message it receives. A concrete walkthrough: create an agency, register two channels, then call setNews. Both channels receive the message. Then register a third channel and send another update. Remove one channel and send a third update; only remaining channels are notified. This sequence demonstrates dynamic subscription and removal. Test cases should assert that observers get correct messages after registration and that removed observers stop receiving messages. Also test edge cases: no observers present, duplicate registration, and thread-safety if you expect concurrent updates. If you expect concurrent modifications, iterating over a copy of the observer list or using concurrent collections avoids ConcurrentModification exceptions. How will you test removal and concurrency in your implementation? In practical terms, read the subject and observer code and see runtime behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Key parts of the NewsAgency example are shown below. Notice the simple list management and notify loop.
<!-- Subject & Observer interfaces -->
interface Subject {
  void registerObserver(Observer o);
  void removeObserver(Observer o);
  void notifyObservers();
}

interface Observer {
  void update(String message);
}

// Partial Concrete Subject
class NewsAgency implements Subject {
  private List<Observer> observers = new ArrayList<>();
  private String news;

  public void setNews(String news) {
    this.news = news;
    notifyObservers();
  }

  @Override
  public void registerObserver(Observer o) { observers.add(o); }

  @Override
  public void removeObserver(Observer o) { observers.remove(o); }

  @Override
  public void notifyObservers() {
    for (Observer o : observers) { o.update(news); }
  }
}
Runtime example
Sequence: create agency; create channels; register channels; call setNews; observe output. Then add/remove channels and observe differences. Include tests asserting printed or returned messages.
Testing tips
  • Assert update was called with expected message on each registered observer.
  • After removeObserver, assert that observer receives no further updates.
  • Test empty observer lists and duplicate registrations.
Reflection: can your Subject be observed by many types of observers? Ensure update payloads remain stable to avoid frequent observer changes.

screens.title: Observer hands-on — Stock Price Notifier starter
screens.narratorSegment: This guided starter turns the Observer pattern into a practical exercise: build a StockMarket subject with StockDisplay and TraderAlert observers. The Subject exposes addObserver, removeObserver, and notifyObservers that pass stock symbol and price. StockDisplay prints the latest price for a symbol. TraderAlert holds a threshold and sends an alert when price exceeds that threshold. The important design decisions are the update signature and observer lifecycle management. Keep the update method minimal: for example, pass the stock symbol and price instead of the entire market state to reduce coupling. Test the system by registering a display and an alert, then calling setStockPrice for symbols like AAPL and GOOG. Observe expected behavior when prices cross thresholds and when removing observers. Also test multiple alerts with different thresholds. Finally, consider thread-safety if price updates may come from multiple threads; simple synchronization or a concurrent collection for observers can prevent race conditions. What tests will you write to validate threshold logic and observer removal? keyIdea.title: Starter task
keyIdea.text: Implement StockMarket subject and observers to practice registration, notification, and removal with concrete examples and tests.

content.html:
Starter Code
// Subject Interface
interface StockSubject {
  void addObserver(StockObserver o);
  void removeObserver(StockObserver o);
  void notifyObservers(String stockSymbol, double price);
}

// Observer Interface
interface StockObserver {
  void update(String stockSymbol, double price);
}

// Partial Concrete Subject
class StockMarket implements StockSubject {
  private List<StockObserver> observers = new ArrayList<>();
  private String currentStockSymbol;
  private double currentPrice;

  public void setStockPrice(String stockSymbol, double price) {
    this.currentStockSymbol = stockSymbol;
    this.currentPrice = price;
    notifyObservers(stockSymbol, price);
  }

  @Override
  public void addObserver(StockObserver o) { observers.add(o); }

  @Override
  public void removeObserver(StockObserver o) { observers.remove(o); }

  @Override
  public void notifyObservers(String stockSymbol, double price) {
    for (StockObserver o : observers) { o.update(stockSymbol, price); }
  }
}
Guidance & tests
Design tests that check display output and threshold alerts. Example: register a TraderAlert with threshold 150, then set AAPL to 155 and assert alert fired. After removing the alert, set AAPL again and assert no alert fired.
Design notes
  • Keep update signature compact: symbol and price.
  • Manage observer lifecycle explicitly in clients to avoid leaks.
  • Use synchronized blocks or a concurrent list if updates are concurrent.
Reflection: how would you add prioritized observers or filter notifications without breaking the Observer contract?

screens.title: Strategy pattern — Roles and intent
screens.narratorSegment: The Strategy pattern defines a family of algorithms, encapsulates each one, and makes them interchangeable. The key parts are the Strategy interface, concrete strategy implementations, and a Context that holds a reference to a strategy and delegates the work. A concrete example from the chapter is a ShoppingCart that delegates discount calculation to a DiscountStrategy. Concrete strategies include PercentageDiscount, FixedAmountDiscount, and NoDiscount. The real benefit is separating algorithm choices from the client: you avoid conditional branches in ShoppingCart and make each algorithm independently testable. A common misconception is to introduce Strategy for trivial, stable behavior — that creates unnecessary classes. Reserve Strategy when algorithms vary, are chosen at runtime, or need independent testing. When implementing in Java, keep the strategy interface small and focused, and supply a sensible default strategy in the Context so behavior remains predictable if no strategy is set. How would you design a new discount strategy to be composable with existing ones? Strategy pattern — Roles and intent means strategy encapsulates algorithms; context delegates to a strategy reference so behavior can change without modifying the context.. In practical terms, context, strategy, and concretestrategy explained. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Strategy roles
keyIdea.text: Strategy encapsulates algorithms; Context delegates to a Strategy reference so behavior can change without modifying the Context.

content.html:
Core Concept
Strategy pattern intent
Encapsulate a family of algorithms behind a common interface so a client can select among them at runtime without changing its own code.
Strategy: an interface for a family of algorithms.
ConcreteStrategy: specific algorithm implementations.
Context: holds a Strategy reference and delegates requests to it.
Key Takeaway

Use Strategy to remove complex conditionals and make each algorithm independently implementable and testable.

ShoppingCart example
ShoppingCart holds a DiscountStrategy and calls applyDiscount to compute final totals. You can change strategy at runtime via setDiscountStrategy, letting clients switch discount behavior without changing ShoppingCart code.
Common mistake
Over-using Strategy for algorithms that rarely change adds boilerplate; prefer in cases where algorithms are swapped, extended, or tested independently.
Reflection: when you add a new discount type, will it require changes to the Context? If not, your design follows the Open/Closed Principle.

screens.title: Strategy — ShoppingCart and DiscountStrategy walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: We'll walk through the ShoppingCart and DiscountStrategy example to highlight delegation and runtime switching. The Strategy interface defines applyDiscount(totalAmount). PercentageDiscount, FixedAmountDiscount, and NoDiscount are concrete strategies implementing the interface. ShoppingCart stores a DiscountStrategy reference and delegates the final amount calculation to it. At construction you might set NoDiscount as the default. During runtime, the client calls setDiscountStrategy with a new strategy object and then calls calculateFinalAmount to compute the discounted total. This separation makes each discount algorithm independently testable: write unit tests that pass different totals to each strategy and assert expected results. A common pitfall is letting strategies maintain state that affects subsequent calculations; prefer stateless strategies or clearly documented stateful ones. Also validate inputs inside strategies, for example preventing negative final totals. Practice by adding a PremiumDiscount strategy that composes other strategies or adds membership checks. How will you design tests to confirm composition behaves correctly? keyIdea.title: Delegation
keyIdea.text: Context delegates algorithmic work to the Strategy implementation, supporting runtime switching and isolated testing.

content.html:
Strategy code
// Strategy interface
interface DiscountStrategy {
  double applyDiscount(double totalAmount);
}

// Concrete strategies
class PercentageDiscount implements DiscountStrategy {
  private double percentage;
  public PercentageDiscount(double percentage) { this.percentage = percentage; }
  @Override
  public double applyDiscount(double totalAmount) { return totalAmount * (1 - percentage); }
}

class FixedAmountDiscount implements DiscountStrategy {
  private double fixedAmount;
  public FixedAmountDiscount(double fixedAmount) { this.fixedAmount = fixedAmount; }
  @Override
  public double applyDiscount(double totalAmount) { return totalAmount - fixedAmount; }

  public void setDiscountStrategy(DiscountStrategy ds) { this.discountStrategy = ds; }
  public double calculateFinalAmount() { return discountStrategy.applyDiscount(totalAmount); }
}

screens.title: Observer vs Strategy — When to use each
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between Observer and Strategy requires focusing on the relationship you need. Use Observer when you have a one-to-many relationship: one subject drives updates and many dependent objects must react, often asynchronously. Practical examples include event systems, UI listeners, and live data feeds. The core property is that the subject broadcasts state changes to interested parties without knowing their concrete types. Use Strategy when a single class needs to vary its internal algorithmic behavior: encapsulate each algorithm behind a common interface and let the context switch strategies at runtime. Think of Strategy for discount calculators, compression algorithms, or sorting strategies. A common confusion is to try to force event-driven notifications into Strategy: they are different concerns. Observer handles communication among objects; Strategy handles internal selection of behavior. Another contrast: Observer often requires lifecycle management and careful attention to listener removal; Strategy usually needs no lifecycle management because strategies are often stateless and short-lived. To pick correctly, ask: do I need to notify many dependents, or do I need to swap algorithms inside a single client? screens.title: Common mistakes and testing strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Practical experience shows a few recurring mistakes when applying these patterns. For Observer, the primary hazard is memory leaks from observers that remain registered after they are no longer needed. The fix is explicit lifecycle management: observers should unregister during teardown or use weak references if the language permits. Also, be mindful of the notification payload; sending the entire subject forces observers to depend on its structure. For Strategy, avoid putting mutable state in strategy objects unless their lifecycle is well controlled; stateless strategies are easier to reuse and test. Overuse of Strategy is another trap: if an algorithm is unlikely to change, adding a strategy adds boilerplate with little benefit. Testing strategies is straightforward because they are small and isolated; write unit tests focusing on algorithm correctness. For observers, write integration-style tests that register mock observers and assert calls to update. If concurrent updates are possible, design tests that simulate concurrent notifications and ensure proper synchronization or use of concurrent collections. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll explore two essential behavioral patterns that control how objects communicate and change behavior. First, Observer establishes a one-to-many relationship so a subject can notify many observers when its state changes. This is the backbone of event-driven systems and GUIs where decoupled updates are required. Second, Strategy isolates algorithms behind a common interface so a client can swap behaviors at runtime without modifying its own code. We'll look closely at Java examples for each pattern and practical use cases where they improve flexibility. You'll see a NewsAgency and news channels demonstrating Observer, and a ShoppingCart with discount strategies demonstrating Strategy. We'll also discuss common mistakes: uncontrolled observer lists leading to memory leaks and overuse of Strategy when algorithms are stable. By the end you'll be able to choose between notifying dependents and encapsulating algorithms, and implement both patterns in small, testable Java classes. Consider how your current projects handle notifications and algorithm choices — could a pattern reduce conditional logic or tighten coupling? That question will guide the hands-on tasks we present next.

These objectives focus on practical implementation and design judgement. First, you'll implement the Observer pattern so a subject can notify multiple observers when its state changes. That matters in event-driven code and GUIs where many components react to a single source without tight coupling. Second, you'll identify appropriate use cases for Observer, such as subscriptions, live feeds, or GUI listeners, and understand the memory-care required when registering and removing observers. Each objective emphasizes both the how and the why. Third, you'll implement the Strategy pattern to encapsulate algorithms and make them interchangeable, reducing conditional branches and improving testability. Fourth, you'll learn to decide between Observer and Strategy by contrasting their roles: Observer manages communication among objects, Strategy manages internal algorithm choice. The skills include writing Java interfaces, concrete implementations, and small client classes that compose patterns safely. You'll practice with live code examples and guided tasks to ensure you can both apply the patterns and recognize when they are unnecessary overhead.

These objectives focus on practical verification and safe use. You should be able to implement the sample NewsAgency and NewsChannel classes so that register, remove, and notify work predictably. Test cases should verify that observers receive updates and that removing an observer stops the notifications. For Strategy, implement different discount strategies and write tests that confirm the ShoppingCart applies the chosen strategy correctly. Also practice a small memory check: ensure observers are removed when no longer needed to avoid preventing garbage collection in long-running programs. Finally, you'll learn to read requirements and decide whether an Observer, a Strategy, or a simple direct implementation is the cleanest solution. The assessment items in this chapter check pattern selection, correct interface design, and simple unit-testable implementations so you can demonstrate mastery in small, focused code samples.

Behavioral patterns focus on object interaction and the assignment of responsibilities. They are not about creating objects or arranging structure; they are about how objects collaborate at runtime. The core claim is simple: by standardizing interaction through small, focused interfaces, your code becomes easier to change and reason about. For example, Observer standardizes notification so subjects and observers are decoupled; Strategy standardizes algorithm selection so clients delegate behavior. A concrete example: in a GUI, an event source does not need to know every listener type—listeners implement a common interface and register themselves. A common misconception is that patterns are a silver bullet that solve all coupling problems. In reality, misuse can add unnecessary indirection: use Strategy only when algorithms interchange or when clients must vary behavior. Similarly, Observer can introduce hidden memory retention if observers are not removed. To apply these patterns, learn their vocabulary: Subject and Observer for publish-subscribe, Strategy and Context for interchangeable algorithms. Practice by writing small interfaces first, then minimal concrete implementations that are easy to test. Which responsibilities in your code could be split into a small interface and a set of interchangeable behaviors?

The Observer pattern defines a one-to-many dependency so that when one object changes state, all its dependents are notified automatically. The vocabulary matters: the Subject (or Publisher) holds a list of Observers (Subscribers). Observers implement a common update method that the Subject calls when its state changes. A concrete example from the chapter is a NewsAgency subject and NewsChannel observers. When NewsAgency. setNews() updates state it calls notifyObservers(), and each NewsChannel. update() handles the message. This promotes loose coupling because the Subject depends only on the Observer interface, not concrete types. A common mistake is leaving observers registered after they are no longer needed; that can keep objects alive and cause memory leaks in long-running applications. Another practical note: choose the notification payload carefully — sending minimal, stable data reduces the need to change both Subject and Observers. To implement Observer in Java, create Subject and Observer interfaces, a concrete subject that maintains a list of observers, and concrete observers that register themselves. Test by registering several observers, updating state, and confirming each observer received the update. What cleanup steps will you include to avoid leaks?

Let's step through the NewsAgency and NewsChannel example to see Observer in practice. The Subject interface declares registerObserver, removeObserver, and notifyObservers. NewsAgency keeps a List of Observer and a news state. When setNews is called it assigns the new string and calls notifyObservers, which iterates over the list and invokes update on each Observer. NewsChannel implements update to print or otherwise react to the message it receives. A concrete walkthrough: create an agency, register two channels, then call setNews. Both channels receive the message. Then register a third channel and send another update. Remove one channel and send a third update; only remaining channels are notified. This sequence demonstrates dynamic subscription and removal. Test cases should assert that observers get correct messages after registration and that removed observers stop receiving messages. Also test edge cases: no observers present, duplicate registration, and thread-safety if you expect concurrent updates. If you expect concurrent modifications, iterating over a copy of the observer list or using concurrent collections avoids ConcurrentModification exceptions. How will you test removal and concurrency in your implementation? In practical terms, read the subject and observer code and see runtime behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

This guided starter turns the Observer pattern into a practical exercise: build a StockMarket subject with StockDisplay and TraderAlert observers. The Subject exposes addObserver, removeObserver, and notifyObservers that pass stock symbol and price. StockDisplay prints the latest price for a symbol. TraderAlert holds a threshold and sends an alert when price exceeds that threshold. The important design decisions are the update signature and observer lifecycle management. Keep the update method minimal: for example, pass the stock symbol and price instead of the entire market state to reduce coupling. Test the system by registering a display and an alert, then calling setStockPrice for symbols like AAPL and GOOG. Observe expected behavior when prices cross thresholds and when removing observers. Also test multiple alerts with different thresholds. Finally, consider thread-safety if price updates may come from multiple threads; simple synchronization or a concurrent collection for observers can prevent race conditions. What tests will you write to validate threshold logic and observer removal? This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The Strategy pattern defines a family of algorithms, encapsulates each one, and makes them interchangeable. The key parts are the Strategy interface, concrete strategy implementations, and a Context that holds a reference to a strategy and delegates the work. A concrete example from the chapter is a ShoppingCart that delegates discount calculation to a DiscountStrategy. Concrete strategies include PercentageDiscount, FixedAmountDiscount, and NoDiscount. The real benefit is separating algorithm choices from the client: you avoid conditional branches in ShoppingCart and make each algorithm independently testable. A common misconception is to introduce Strategy for trivial, stable behavior — that creates unnecessary classes. Reserve Strategy when algorithms vary, are chosen at runtime, or need independent testing. When implementing in Java, keep the strategy interface small and focused, and supply a sensible default strategy in the Context so behavior remains predictable if no strategy is set. How would you design a new discount strategy to be composable with existing ones? This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

We'll walk through the ShoppingCart and DiscountStrategy example to highlight delegation and runtime switching. The Strategy interface defines applyDiscount(totalAmount). PercentageDiscount, FixedAmountDiscount, and NoDiscount are concrete strategies implementing the interface. ShoppingCart stores a DiscountStrategy reference and delegates the final amount calculation to it. At construction you might set NoDiscount as the default. During runtime, the client calls setDiscountStrategy with a new strategy object and then calls calculateFinalAmount to compute the discounted total. This separation makes each discount algorithm independently testable: write unit tests that pass different totals to each strategy and assert expected results. A common pitfall is letting strategies maintain state that affects subsequent calculations; prefer stateless strategies or clearly documented stateful ones. Also validate inputs inside strategies, for example preventing negative final totals. Practice by adding a PremiumDiscount strategy that composes other strategies or adds membership checks. How will you design tests to confirm composition behaves correctly? The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Choosing between Observer and Strategy requires focusing on the relationship you need. Use Observer when you have a one-to-many relationship: one subject drives updates and many dependent objects must react, often asynchronously. Practical examples include event systems, UI listeners, and live data feeds. The core property is that the subject broadcasts state changes to interested parties without knowing their concrete types. Use Strategy when a single class needs to vary its internal algorithmic behavior: encapsulate each algorithm behind a common interface and let the context switch strategies at runtime. Think of Strategy for discount calculators, compression algorithms, or sorting strategies. A common confusion is to try to force event-driven notifications into Strategy: they are different concerns. Observer handles communication among objects; Strategy handles internal selection of behavior. Another contrast: Observer often requires lifecycle management and careful attention to listener removal; Strategy usually needs no lifecycle management because strategies are often stateless and short-lived. Practical experience shows a few recurring mistakes when applying these patterns. For Observer, the primary hazard is memory leaks from observers that remain registered after they are no longer needed. The fix is explicit lifecycle management: observers should unregister during teardown or use weak references if the language permits. Also, be mindful of the notification payload; sending the entire subject forces observers to depend on its structure. For Strategy, avoid putting mutable state in strategy objects unless their lifecycle is well controlled; stateless strategies are easier to reuse and test. Overuse of Strategy is another trap: if an algorithm is unlikely to change, adding a strategy adds boilerplate with little benefit. Testing strategies is straightforward because they are small and isolated; write unit tests focusing on algorithm correctness. For observers, write integration-style tests that register mock observers and assert calls to update. If concurrent updates are possible, design tests that simulate concurrent notifications and ensure proper synchronization or use of concurrent collections. Let's summarize three compact ideas to remember. First: Observer implements a one-to-many dependency so a Subject can notify registered Observers when its state changes. This is ideal for event-driven or UI systems, but remember to manage observer lifecycles to avoid leaks. Second: Strategy encapsulates algorithms behind a common interface, letting a Context switch behaviors at runtime without internal conditional complexity. Strategies are easy to unit test and often stateless. Third: Choose patterns intentionally. Use Observer when multiple dependents must react to a source; use Strategy when a single client must change behavior. Avoid adding patterns where plain, clear code suffices.
